1:
Gill spends his comment refusing a reading. Some take the vision of a glorious state of the church begun in the apostles' own time, when the old Jewish order passed and a new dispensation took its place; but death did not then cease, having reigned ever since, and instead of sorrow and sighing fleeing away there was for three hundred years scarce anything else. Wesley places it after the resurrection and the general judgment, and insists that John is not describing a flourishing state of the church but a new and eternal state of all things. Henry thinks it safest to understand the heavenly state, and reads the new earth as a condition for the bodies of men as the new heaven is for their souls; this world is not newly created but newly opened, and the very earth of the saints, their glorified bodies, will be spiritual and heavenly, suited to those bright mansions. Barnes sets out the whole chapter as one picture: the redeemed after the judgment, drawn under the image of a beautiful city, of which Jerusalem was the emblem — a city with no temple, for it is all a temple, and needing no light, for God is its light.

The word that governs the description is new, and Ellicott takes it apart. Greek has two words so translated, one relating to time and the other to quality; the tomb in which our Lord was laid was new not because it had lately been hewn but because it had never been used, and the wine-skins wanted for new wine were not freshly made but unwithered; both are described by the second word. That second word is the one used throughout this chapter and throughout the book, so the newness pictured is the newness of freshness, the old and decaying and corrupting elements being swept away. He draws a consequence from it: all things may be new and yet not strange, since there must be some correspondency between the old and the new when the new things are called new heavens, new earth, new Jerusalem. The hope itself, he adds, was long cherished, sanctioned by Isaiah, closed by Ezekiel with his vision of a renewed land, and named by Christ the regeneration. Clarke reports the rabbinic form of the same expectation, that God would renew the heavens and the earth at the end of seven thousand years, and then refuses to speculate, quoting Calmet that to pretend to say what this new heaven and new earth are, and what their ornaments and qualities, is the greatest of all presumptions.

On the sea the interpreters divide by method rather than by result. Ellicott would render it that the sea exists no more, and finds it strange that so many commentators vacillate, treating the ornaments of the city as symbolical while taking the annihilation of the sea as literal; wiser, he says, to leave the literal meaning to the future and grasp the spiritual teaching, remembering how the sea has served the symbolism of this book, since out of it rose the wild beast, on many waters sat the purple-clad Babylon, and the troubled sea of evil cannot rest but casts up mire and dirt. Robertson agrees on the method and differs on the scope: this is not a picture of the renovation of this earth but of the disappearance of this earth and sky, though not of the heaven where God dwells; and while the symbolism is not to be pressed too literally, a stern and a glorious reality lies behind it all. Clarke supposes the sea was made new with the rest and probably differently placed and distributed. Wesley notices that the verb here is milder than the one used three verses later: death and mourning and sorrow go away altogether, whereas the former heaven and earth only pass away, giving place to the new.
2:
Gill takes the city for the whole body of the elect rather than the militant church, the general assembly and church of the firstborn, and calls them holy in a sense not yet true, since they will be perfectly holy in themselves, without the being of sin in them or any spot of it upon them. Robertson quotes Swete that the new earth must have a new metropolis, not another Babylon but a greater Jerusalem, and not the old city destroyed in the year seventy; it was called the holy city conventionally, and now is so in reality. Barnes insists the descent cannot be pressed, since a city three hundred and seventy miles high, made of gold, with single pearls for gates, cannot literally settle on the earth; and he notes that Scripture commonly likens a city to a beautiful woman, the two images being here combined. Ellicott makes the direction of movement the point. She is seen not rising out of earth or sea, like the foes of righteousness earlier in the book, but coming down from heaven: the world will never evolve a golden age or an ideal state, and the true pattern is the pattern in the mount. Clarke reports the rabbinic form of the same expectation, that tabernacle and temple and Jerusalem came down from heaven, and that God would renew the world and cause Jerusalem to descend, the Jewish opinion being that these subsist in spiritual representatives and so cannot be destroyed. Wesley adds that the city belongs neither to this world nor to the millennium but to eternity, and is caught in the very act of descending.

On the voice that follows, Ellicott prefers the best manuscripts, which have it out of the throne, and presses the tent that lies in the word, since to render it dwell weakens the allusion. He marks a change of preposition from an earlier chapter, where God tabernacles over his people, whereas here he tabernacles with them, not merely stretching his cloud-shelter above them but present among them; and he objects to the words supplied in italics in our version, the force being that they are his people and he their Emmanuel, God with them. Robertson takes the metaphor back to the Shekinah glory of the old tabernacle, a picture of the true one, and says God is now Immanuel in fact, as was true of Christ. Barnes adds that the tabernacle was regarded as God's peculiar dwelling-place, and that the text does not say this will be on the earth, though he thinks the earth may yet become an abode of the redeemed.

The promise about tears is read closely. Ellicott would render every tear rather than all tears, and counts the negatives that follow as heralds of positive peace — no sea, no tears, no death, no mourning, no crying, no pain, six shadows departing with the former things. He defines them from Trench: the mourning is grief which so takes possession of the whole being that it cannot be hid, the crying is the loud outcry witnessing that the times are out of joint, and the pain includes painful labour and weariness. Robertson renders the verb more exactly as wiping every tear out of their eyes, like a tender mother. Barnes measures the promise against the world it is given in, where no one rises in the morning certain he may not end the day in grief, and where the redeemed will never follow a friend to the tomb nor see the soil open its bosom to furnish a grave. Clarke draws a doctrinal inference: death cannot be destroyed merely by there being no further dying, but only by a general resurrection, so this promise both assures the resurrection and proves that after it death will not return. Wesley takes the clause as full proof that the description belongs not to time but to eternity.
5:
Who speaks is not agreed. Gill weighs the Father against Christ and leans to Christ, since the speaker calls himself Alpha and Omega as Christ does elsewhere, and it is he who gives thirsty souls the water of life. Barnes treats the title as decisive, making it morally certain that the speaker is the Lord Jesus and proving him divine, since two verses later he undertakes to be a God to the overcomer. Robertson reads it as the first time since the opening chapter that God speaks directly, and notes that the message is addressed not to John, as other messages in the book are, but to the entire world of the blessed. On the words that follow he suspects a change of speakers, probably an angel bidding John write, and observes that the two adjectives used of the saying are applied elsewhere to God himself and to Christ, so the words are reliable and genuine. Wesley agrees that the angel gives the order, and thinks the apostle had ceased writing, overcome with ecstasy at the voice of him that spake. Ellicott would render the promise as a present, I am making all things new, and hears the assurance of the Throned One who has presided over all the changing scenes of earth's history: in spite of the moral disorder and dark shadows of life, the new creation is preparing and will rise, as the first did, out of chaos.

The declaration that follows is rendered several ways. Ellicott prefers they have come to pass, and counts the assurance trebly sure, adding Bengel's observation that this book says it is done twice, once at the completion of the wrath of God and here at the making of all things new. Barnes hears an echo of the cross: the great work is accomplished, the redeemed gathered in, the wicked cut off, all prepared for the eternal state. Gill fills out the list: the whole election of grace is completed and every vessel of mercy called, the bodies of the saints raised and the living changed, and what was finished on the cross by way of impetration is now done as to application. Robertson keeps God the speaker and divides the title, the beginning being the First Cause and the end the Finality, though the whole is applied to Christ in the last chapter. Wesley takes the second phrase as explaining the first, so that both mean the Everlasting.

The two promises are read as one movement. Ellicott finds in the title the ground of the offer to the thirsty, since he who begins the good work will perform it, and the unsatisfied yearnings of the heart find their satisfaction in him; the gift is free, without money and without price, so he who brings everything brings nothing, and he who brings nothing brings everything. Clarke shows the same expectation among the rabbins, who counted the fountain of the world to come among the blessings of a future state, and imagined the lost crying, Wo to us, what good have we lost. Robertson marks the promise as God's own, and its partitive form, a draught out of the fountain. On the overcomer, Ellicott reads these things rather than all things, and hears the echo of the promises to the seven churches, the weapons of victory having been named already as the blood of the Lamb, the word of their testimony and the victory of faith. Robertson traces the two clauses of the adoption, the first a promise made to Abraham and the second a word spoken of Solomon and applied afterwards to David. Wesley observes that to overcome is more than to thirst, and adds a grammarian's caution: shall and will are one word in both Hebrew and Greek, the difference lying in the English, or in the want of knowledge in him who interprets what he does not understand.
8:
The first name on the list is qualified before it is applied. Gill will not have it touch the timorous sheep and lambs of Christ, who are often of a fearful heart on account of sin and temptation and unbelief, but only those of cowardly spirits who are not valiant for the truth, who through fear of men either make no profession of Christ or drop the one they made lest they be exposed to persecution — men afraid of the beast and in servile bondage to him. Clarke describes the same men historically, as those who for fear of losing life or property refused a religion they were convinced was true, or having received it fell away when it grew dangerous. Barnes sets them expressly against the overcomer of the verse before, as those who had not firmness to avow their professed principles in a wicked world. Ellicott divides the word, since there is a high and holy fear in which the Christian passes the time of his sojourn here, and a base and selfish fear of man which brings a snare; the cowardly sink into companionship with the faithless. Robertson makes the second epithet mean untrustworthy rather than merely unbelieving, set against Christ who is called the faithful, and adds that disloyalty is close kin to cowardice.

The rest of the catalogue is glossed term by term. Barnes derives the word for the abominable from a verb meaning to excite disgust, so that it covers all whose conduct is offensive to God and fitted to excite abhorrence. Robertson takes the same word as pollution and refers it to those defiled by the impurities of emperor-worship. Clarke defines the sorcerers as persons who by drugs, philtres and fumigations pretend to produce supernatural effects, and the idolaters as those who offer any kind of worship to anything but God, adding that all image worshippers are idolaters in every sense of the word. On the last term he is strictest of all, since it takes in every one who speaks contrary to the truth while knowing it, and even the man who speaks the truth meaning to deceive, by telling only part of it or suppressing a circumstance that would have led the hearer to a different conclusion. Barnes reaches the same breadth more briefly, taking in all who are false in their statements, their promises and their contracts, false towards God and false towards men, and Robertson observes that lying is stigmatised again and again in this book and is not a light sin. Wesley disposes of three together, since fornication, sorcery and idolatry generally went in company.

Ellicott finds an arrangement in the list. The less glaring faults stand first, and the characters have been thought to form four pairs: fear and unbelief, which go hand in hand; the workers of abomination and the murderers; the fornicators and the sorcerers, as those who sin in secret; and the idolaters and the false, as those who change God's truth into a lie. Robertson counts eight epithets, all in the same case, describing what Charles called those who have disfranchised themselves from the Kingdom of God, and places them with Satan and the two beasts among the names not found in the book of life. Ellicott closes with a qualification the list itself does not make. Those shut out stand in contrast with those admitted, and yet among the admitted are men who have sinned through fear and faithlessness and fleshliness; sin indeed excludes from the city, but it is sin loved and unrepented of which alone can close the gate of a city whose gates lie open day and night. Clarke adds a textual note, that about thirty excellent manuscripts, with the Syriac and the Arabic, insert sinners into the list, on which evidence Griesbach admitted the word into his text.
9:
The messenger is chosen for the contrast he makes. Ellicott notes that one of the seven angels which had the vials of wrath had shown the seer the scarlet-clad harlot, the guilty Babylon, and that one of the same company now shows him the pure Bride, the new and holy Jerusalem. Robertson makes the same point of the introduction, which repeats the announcement about the harlot city word for word, so that the Bride is set in sharp contrast with her; he adds that the title wife is proleptic, the marriage not yet being a reality. Wesley puts it in a line: the same angel had before showed him Babylon, which is directly opposed to the new Jerusalem. Barnes cannot say why one of these angels was employed, but suggests that since they had brought destruction on the enemies of the church, it was fitting that its triumph should be announced by one of them. Henry generalises from the choice, that God has a variety of work for his holy angels: sometimes they are to sound the trumpet of divine providence and give fair warning to a careless world, sometimes to pour out the vials of his anger upon impenitent sinners, and sometimes to discover things of a heavenly nature to the heirs of salvation.

The carrying away is understood of the mind rather than the body. Gill says John was in an ecstasy, so that it only seemed to him as if he were taken from place to place, none of these visions being corporeal sights but things represented to his spirit, as with Paul caught up to the third heaven, who could not tell whether he was in the body or out of it; and he notes that the Ethiopic version makes the Spirit the agent, not the evil spirit who once carried our Lord bodily to an exceeding high mountain. Robertson finds the same removal in Ezekiel, and thinks the mountain cannot be Zion, since the new Jerusalem is seen descending from it. Barnes and Clarke keep to the practical use of the height, which gave an unobstructed view, so that being above the city he might see every street and lane of it. Ellicott will not stop there. The glimpse of God's coming glories is best gained from the consecrated heights of self-surrender and prayer, on a mountain apart from the world, and there are heights of vision and transfiguration from which such sights are had.

What was shown is measured against two other sights. Ellicott sets the scene beside the temptation: the tempter showed our Lord the kingdoms of the world and the glory of them, while the comforting angel shows our Lord's prophet the city which hath the foundations, and the glory of it. Wesley compares the older vision, since Ezekiel also describes a holy city, and the two agree in many particulars but differ in more, the prophet describing the temple and its worship in close allusion to the Levitical service, whereas John saw no temple and describes a city far larger and more heavenly; and he notices that the old city is now so forgotten that this one is no longer called the new Jerusalem but simply Jerusalem. Henry reads the subject as the church in her perfect and triumphant state, comely through the comeliness put upon her by her husband, glorious in her relation to Christ and in his image now perfected in her. He draws the practical rule from the vantage point: those who would have clear views of heaven must get as near heaven as they can, into the mount of vision, the mount of meditation and faith, whence, as from the top of Pisgah, they may behold the goodly land of the heavenly Canaan. Wesley adds what the sight cost the seer: O how did St John long to enter in, but the time was not yet come.
11:
Gill takes the glory two ways at once. It rests on the saints themselves, whose bodies will be freed from dishonour and disease and made like Christ's glorious body, and it means also the presence of God, the Shechinah that filled tabernacle and temple; if the faces of Moses and Stephen shone so brightly at that presence, how much more shall the saints shine in this state. Ellicott agrees that the glory is the true Shechinah, and notes that the word for the city's brightness is the light which she gives, the same word used in the Greek of Genesis for the heavenly bodies. Robertson calls it a luminary, a word found in the New Testament only here and where Paul bids Christians shine as lights, and quotes Swete that the luminary of the Holy City is her witness to Christ. Barnes traces the same word to its ordinary use, where it means a light-giver and in profane writers commonly a window, and takes it here for the brightness of the divine glory supplying the place of sun or window. Wesley presses the figure of the window and makes it a single one running all the way round the city: the light does not come in from without, since the glory of God is within, but shines out from within to a great distance.

The stone is described by its optics. Clarke observes that among precious stones some of the same species are far more valuable, their worth being in proportion as they are free from flaws and of a good water; a crystal is perfectly clear and the oriental jasper a beautiful sea-green, and what is described here is a jasper perfectly transparent. He then explains why the tint matters: the light of this city is intense, equal and splendid, but tinged with green to make it agreeable to the sight, since nothing is so friendly to the eye as blue or green, while other colours fatigue and, if intense, injure it, these being the colours of earth and sky to which the eye is adapted. Ellicott reaches the same picture from the throne-vision, the general brightness being lustrous as the diamond but shot with the green tint of the emerald bow which swept the throne. Barnes adds that the stone is essentially a quartz and comes red, yellow and brown, so that the word crystal is put in to show which sort is meant.

On the wall Gill canvasses the interpretations and settles on the plainest. It is not the Spirit of God, nor the eternal decree; many take it for the doctrine of the gospel, great because of its great Author and high because carnal minds cannot reach it; but he thinks it means rather the almighty power of God, which guards his people now and will be their defence then. Barnes keeps to the architecture, since ancient cities were always walled, and great means thick and strong; and he gives the angels at the gates a duty, to watch that nothing improper should enter, and that the great enemy should not make an insidious approach as he did to the earthly Paradise. Robertson notes that the word is used through this book for the gate tower rather than the door, and that the twelve are stationed as watchmen after the manner of Isaiah's prophecy. Clarke reports a rabbinic parallel from the Sohar, that in the palace of the world to come there are twelve gates inscribed with the names of the tribes, and that he who is of the tribe of Reuben is received at none of them but his own. Wesley says only that the angels are still waiting upon the heirs of salvation. Barnes finds no special significance in the threes except access from every quarter, since those who dwell there will have come from each of the great divisions of the earth.
14:
Gill keeps the doctrine straight before counting stones: Christ is the one and only foundation, and the twelve are named only because he was ministerially laid by the twelve apostles; the plural also marks the firm state of a church which is a city that has foundations. Ellicott sees the whole Church of both Testaments in the city, with the apostles' work given special recognition, since it is on their teaching and witness that the great spiritual Jerusalem is built, in complete harmony with what Paul writes to the Ephesians. He turns aside to an objection, that John could not have written the book since he reckons the apostles, himself among them, as foundation-stones; the same argument would tell with equal wisdom against Paul's authorship of Ephesians, and betrays a misapprehension of the value of symbols. Robertson observes that all twelve names are written and not Peter's only, as some would argue, Christ being the corner stone rather than a foundation among the rest; and he wonders aloud whether the name on the twelfth stone is Judas or Matthias. Clarke supposes twelve stones, one serving as threshold to each gate, to intimate that souls enter the Church by the doctrine of the apostles, and Wesley reads it as showing that the inhabitants built only on the faith once delivered to the saints. Barnes prefers twelve courses laid one above another to twelve stones set at intervals, the latter arrangement suggesting feebleness.

The measuring rod is noticed for its metal. Barnes says it is of gold because everything about the city is of the most costly materials, so that the instrument suits the person using it and the occasion, and its object is to show the city's proper proportions. Ellicott contrasts it with the reed of an earlier chapter, which was not said to be gold and whose measuring symbolised preservation amid impending danger, whereas this measuring exhibits the beauty and proportion of a city now dwelling at peace; gold may stand as the token of the wealth of a royal city, though the wealth of this city is love. Robertson simply notes that a rod of gold was in keeping with the dignity of the service of God. Clarke adds that several excellent manuscripts insert a word making it explicitly a measuring rod, and that the whole account seems copied with variations from Ezekiel.

The square is where the interpreters part company with the literalists. Barnes explains what regularity means here, since most cities take their outline from hills or streams or grow by accretion until the plan is lost sight of, whereas this one was built to a plan that circumstances never modified; the height of three hundred and seventy-five miles precludes any literal city in Palestine, and the point of such vastness is that the numbers of the redeemed will be immense. Wesley measures it against real cities, Jerusalem being thirty-three furlongs round and Babylon four hundred and eighty, and asks what inconsiderable villages these were by comparison; he warns that a deep reverence is necessary in treating such things, that we may neither understand them too literally and grossly nor go too far from the natural force of the words. Robertson notes that Herodotus made Babylon a square and Diodorus said the same of Nineveh, and that this city is a perfect cube like the holy of holies in Solomon's temple; it is useless to reduce the measurements, the meaning being that heaven will be large enough for all. Clarke finds the quadrangular form a token of perfection and stability, the square being among the Greeks a figure of perfection, so that the square man was one of unsullied integrity. Ellicott is briskest: many are nervously anxious about the monstrous appearance of such a city, but there is no need to be nervous about symbols, and attempts to paint them end only in grotesque and profane pictures.
17:
Gill takes the number back to its root, since twelve times twelve is a hundred and forty-four, and that number is mystical and apostolical and suited to the perfect state of this church — whence the twelve gates and their twelve angels, the twelve tribes and the twelve foundations. Robertson agrees it is another multiple of twelve, and is not sure whether height or breadth is meant, though the word for height stands just before; at eighteen inches to the cubit it makes two hundred and sixteen feet, which is nothing beside the fifteen hundred miles of the city itself. Barnes makes the same reckoning and compares Babylon, whose walls Herodotus put at three hundred and fifty feet, so that this height gives every proper idea of security while the city towers immensely above it, its glory not obscured by the wall thrown round it for defence. Clarke explains the unit, the cubit being named from the elbow and reaching to the tip of the middle finger, generally reckoned at a foot and a half though the pyramids suggest twenty-one inches in some cases; and he offers an arithmetical conceit, that if the measuring man and his rod stood six feet, then twenty-four, the number of the tribes and the apostles together, multiplied by six gives precisely a hundred and forty-four.

The clause about the measurer is read as a safeguard. Barnes says it is added to prevent mistake, since an angel is measuring and might be supposed to use some measure not in common use among men, so that no definite idea of the size could be formed. Robertson puts it in Bengel's phrase, man's measure which is angel's. Ellicott presses the doubleness further: the measure is true for men and true for angels, and while it may mean only that the angel used the ordinary human standard, it may also imply that the vision is true for all, earthly and heavenly alike, so that the human will not find the picture untrue though the city is not literal. It is figurative, he says, but not mere figure; and the recurrence of the number recalls us to the figurative character of the whole description.

The materials are read the same way. Gill makes the jasper expressive of the impregnableness and duration and brightness of salvation by Christ, being a stone very hard and durable and bright, and Clarke confirms the mineralogy, since the oriental jasper is almost indestructible and pillars made of it have suffered scarcely anything from the tooth of time. Wesley states the arrangement plainly, that the wall was built of jasper and the houses were of pure gold, and Robertson adds that the city shone like a mass of gold against the jasper lustre of the wall. Clarke then turns on the popular use of the passage. It has been most injudiciously applied to heaven, so that we hear of golden walls and pavements and gates of pearl, without considering that nothing of this was ever intended literally, and that gold and jewels can have no place in a spiritual and eternal world; in symbols they are proper, but construed into realities they are very improper, and such preaching only keeps up a fondness for gold. Ellicott gives the symbol its sense from Lange, that gold has an inalienable reference to the sun and so to the manifestation of God's love: the wealth of heaven is love, all who tread those streets move along the ways of love, and no dimness of self-interest mars the lustre, so that the gold is clear as pure glass. Barnes reaches for a modern illustration and quotes an eye-witness of the Crystal Palace, which at noon resembled a regal palace of silver, at evening was transformed into a temple of gold and rubies, and by moonlight showed an immense surface of glass like a sea.
19:
Gill begins by ruling out readings. The sense is not that every foundation held all manner of precious stones, but that each had its own; nor are the stones to be applied to the persons of the apostles, who were not the foundations but only had their names written on them, especially as their order is not the same in the Evangelists and in the Acts. Still less will he allow Brightman's fancy that they mean ministers of the latter day who shall convert the Jews in the countries where these stones are found. Clarke takes the foundations for the thresholds of the gates, one under each, and reads the whole arrangement as a scheme of the two dispensations: the gates are the twelve tribes and the thresholds the twelve apostles, so that there is no entrance but through those gates and none but over these thresholds. The Mosaic dispensation was the preparation for the gospel, which without it would have no original, as the law without the gospel would have no proper object. Wesley recalls what the same stones meant on the high priest's breastplate, where they were an emblem of the happiness of God's church in his presence and protection, and notices that here each stone is not the ornament of a foundation but the foundation.

The stones are then identified as far as the interpreters can manage it. Barnes traces several of the names to their origins: the chalcedony from a town in Asia Minor opposite Byzantium where the stone was probably first known, the topaz from a small island in the Arabian Gulf, the chrysoprasus from the words for gold and a leek, and the amethyst from a word meaning not to be intoxicated, the gem having been supposed an antidote against drunkenness. He notes that the beryl is identical with the emerald but for the colour, the richer green coming from a trace of chrome. Clarke and Wesley give the shades: the sardonyx red streaked with white, the sardius a deep blood red, the chrysolite dusky green with a cast of yellow, the topaz pale yellow, the jacinth a dead red mixed with yellow, and the amethyst violet, compounded of a strong blue and a deep red. Robertson sorts the whole list by Swete into four families — blue, green, red and yellow — while allowing that even so there is great variety of hue and brilliancy, and that the stones react upon each other.

What the variety is for divides them. Robertson denies that the list carries any necessary mystical meaning, quoting Moffatt that the writer is simply trying to convey the impression of a radiant and superb structure; the gems answer closely, though only eight exactly, to the stones of the breastplate, and Charles's identification of them with the signs of the zodiac in reverse order he calls a needless performance, though he is willing to entertain Clement of Alexandria's suggestion that the variety illustrates the variety of gifts and graces in the twelve apostles. Ellicott makes more of it. He sets the adorned Bride against the harlot, whose robe was decked with gold and precious stones and pearls, and finds these ornaments richer and rarer than the world-mistress wore, so that he who passes by the dazzling attractions of the world wins the true spiritual riches. In the diversity itself he hears the doctrine of gifts differing while the Lord is the same: in the heavenly city there is harmony, not monotony, variety, not sameness, unity, not uniformity. Since the stones are ranged not in the order of the breastplate but by their shades of colour, he sees them encircling the city as with a rainbow belt, with hues that betoken the advent of morning; and he closes with Lange, that as twelve they indicate completeness, as sharing one lustre their unity, and as differing in hue their manifoldness.
21:
Gill reads the pearls as a double emblem, of the preciousness of Christ by whom the saints enter, and of the saints who enter by him. Barnes will not have the gates taken literally, the point being ornament and magnificence, and adds that the street was paved with gold, all the space not built on being of that metal. Clarke says plainly that it is out of the order of nature to produce a pearl large enough for a gate to such a city, but supposes John may be alluding to what his countrymen said of prodigious pearls; and he tells their story of the disciple who laughed at his master for teaching that God would provide gems thirty cubits every way for those gates, asking where such could be found when the largest known was no bigger than a pigeon's egg, and who afterwards, at sea, saw the ministering angels cutting gems and was told they were for the gates of Jerusalem. Ellicott finds a doctrine in the contrast. The foundations are diverse and the gates are alike, so that there is one way though many roads, one mode of entrance through twelve openings. The pearl was reckoned the most valuable of stones among the ancients and is a fit emblem of the highest truth, and so of him who is the Truth as well as the Way; Bacon compared truth to a pearl that showeth best by day, and it is the only precious stone the art of man cannot improve, since the artificer may give fresh lustre to emerald and sapphire but must lift no tool upon the pearl. Robertson notes that the word for the street is singular but covers them all, and that the word for transparent occurs nowhere else in the book.

What is missing from the city is dwelt on as much as what is in it. Gill lists the absences: no material temple as in the old Jerusalem, none such as Ezekiel described, and no place of public worship as under the gospel, since there will be no preaching or administering of ordinances in that state; the Jews expect a third temple, he adds, but in vain. Clarke gives the reason in a line, that there was no need of a temple where God and the Lamb were manifestly present. Barnes turns the absence into a positive, since the city was all temple and nothing but a temple: not like Jerusalem, where one house was reared for worship and the inhabitants repaired to it, but one great temple in honour of God's name, with worship ascending from every part. Robertson makes the same point as a reversal: where the apostle elsewhere calls us the sanctuary of God, here God is our sanctuary, and so is the Lamb.

Ellicott draws out what this implies for everything that now serves religion. In Ezekiel's vision the vast proportions of the temple formed a conspicuous part, and their size declared them figurative; but this vision passes to a higher state of things, in which the age of the Church triumphing succeeds the age of the Church toiling, and the external organisations and instrumentalities required for edifying the body of Christ are no longer needed. Tongues and prophecies and knowledge may pass away, churches disappear, absorbed in the one glorious Church, and ministries and missionary organisations cease; every merely local aspect of worship is at an end, for the Lord is there. Henry says the same: perfect and direct communion with God will more than supply the place of gospel institutions, and he asks what words could more fully express the union and co-equality of the Son with the Father. Wesley states the presence rather than the loss, that God fills the new heaven and the new earth, surrounds the city and sanctifies it and all that are in it, and is all in all.
23:
Gill allows the clause a literal sense, since the luminaries every earthly city needs may still be in being without having the use they now have, and he cites the Jewish saying that the orb of the sun belongs to this world and not to the future state, where the lights shall be renewed. Clarke reports the same tradition, that in the world to come the Israelites shall have no need of the sun by day nor the moon by night, and adds that God's light shines in this city and is concentrated in the Lamb, from whom it is everywhere diffused. Robertson puts it as a comparison of brightness: if sun and moon did shine they would add no light in the presence of the Shekinah Glory, their splendour being put to shame by the glory of God himself. He reports two readings of the second clause, Charles taking the lamp as predicate and Bousset finding a contrast with the moon as the lesser light, which he thinks unnecessary, and prefers Swete's view of Christ as the one lamp over against the many lampstands of the churches on earth, words which show the purely spiritual character of the conception. Wesley says only that the glory is infinitely brighter than the sun. Ellicott notices which title is used, since the emblem of the Lamb recurs here as before: the memory of Christ's work on earth is never obliterated, and in the splendour of that city the remembrance of him who was led as a lamb to the slaughter gives depth and fulness to its joy.

The nations walking in that light are variously limited. Gill will not have all the nations of the world meant, since all will not be saved, nor the Gentiles only, but all the elect of God called out of every nation of the earth. Ellicott follows the best manuscripts in dropping the qualifying words, and sets the vision against the writer's circumstances: the prophet looks out from the loneliness and depression of churches then persecuted and despised, and in the vision sees her enlarged and honoured, all peoples flocking within the walls, which is the echo of the ancient promise that all kings shall fall down before him. Barnes takes the glory brought in to mean whatever the kings reckon their glory, treasures and crowns and robes, all laid at the feet of the Saviour. Wesley qualifies it, that this is not their old glory, which is now abolished, but such as becomes the new earth and receives an immense addition by their entrance. Robertson leaves the question open, reporting Swete's uncertainty whether this is a picture of heaven itself or of some gracious purpose of God towards humanity not yet revealed, and judging the picture beautiful and glorious in either case.

On the gates that are never shut the readings differ in scope. Gill takes it for the safety of the inhabitants rather than free traffic between the risen and the living, since they will have no enemy to fear and need never shut their gates, the beast and the false prophet having long since been cast into the lake of fire. Clarke reads it of the present Church, which stands ever open to receive sinners of all sorts and degrees and nations. Barnes turns the clause the other way, so that the dwellers there are not prisoners: the universe will be open to them, to go forth and visit every world and survey the works of God in all parts of his dominions. Robertson notes the plain reason given for mentioning the day alone, that there shall be no night there. Barnes takes that clause too as more than physical, since it means no literal darkness and nothing of which night is the emblem — no calamity, no sorrow, no bereavement, no windows darkened for the loss of friends and kindred.
26:
Gill reads the glory of the nations as the people of God themselves, who though reckoned the filth of the world are the excellent in the earth, and who will be presented to the King by the kings of the earth — either by ecclesiastical rulers, introducing them as their joy and crown of rejoicing, or by political governors who had been their fathers and protectors. He offers a second sense, that whatever is great and glorious among the nations will count as nothing beside the magnificence of this state, and notes that the Arabic turns the clause about, making the nations bring glory and honour to the city. Wesley supposes a select part of each nation is meant, so that everything which can make the city honourable shall be found in it, as if all that was precious throughout the world were gathered into one place. Robertson makes the comparison with the city already fallen, since Rome gathered the merchandise of the world, whereas the City of God will have the best of all the nations. Clarke keeps the prophetic background in view, the promise being that the Gentiles should contribute their gifts to the riches and glory of the temple. Barnes states the sum in a sentence: that blessed world will be made up of all that was truly valuable and pure on the earth.

What may not enter is stated as strongly as what may. Gill takes the defilement to be evil thoughts and words and actions, notes that the Vulgate and Syriac read that which is defiled and the Arabic that which is unclean, and finds an allusion to the temple, into which no unclean person might come; neither the profane sinner whose conversation defiles, he adds, nor the self-righteous man whose righteousness is filthy rags, but only those washed in the blood of Christ. Barnes points out that the word is literally anything common, and that the negative is of the strongest kind, denoting absolute exclusion. Robertson confirms the usage, the word meaning profane rather than shared by all. Ellicott sets the exclusion beside the open gates: they stand open always, and yet no evil thing may find a home there, which is in harmony with all Scripture, since no unholiness can dwell in the presence of God; the allusion is to the care of the Jews in keeping every unclean thing from the sanctuary, a ceremonial rule whose spiritual significance the apostles used elsewhere.

The two pictures raise a question Robertson leaves standing. These recurrent glimpses of pagan life on earth and of hell set against heaven make it uncertain whether John runs parallel pictures of the two after the judgment, or whether, as Charles puts it, the unclean and the abominable and the liars are still on earth and cannot enter though the gates stand open day and night; in apocalyptic writing, he adds, literalism and chronology cannot be insisted on, and the panoramas continue to the end. Clarke turns the exclusion on the reader instead. He defines the impure man as one who turns the grace of God into lasciviousness, the liar as one who holds and propagates false doctrines, reminds every Christian that his baptism bound him to renounce the devil and all his works, the pomps and vanities of this wicked world, and asks plainly whether the reader is of that number, or is expecting an eternal glory while living in sin; presuming on the mercy of God, he warns, is as ruinous as despairing of his grace, and where God gives power both to will and to do, a man should work out his own salvation with fear and trembling. Wesley closes on the register rather than the warning: the blessedness belongs to true and holy and persevering believers, who as such are written among them that are to inherit eternal life.
